title: Nichesss Review: 150 Templates for a One-Time Price
description: Nichesss sells 150+ single-task writing templates and a long-form editor for a $59 lifetime deal. What the template model is good at, and where it shows.
content:
# Nichesss Review: 150 Templates for a One-Time Price

AI writing tools come in two shapes. One is a chat box that will do anything if you describe it well enough. The other is a library of narrow templates that will do one thing without being asked twice. [[link:/tools/1441|Nichesss]] is firmly the second kind, and the whole product makes sense only once you accept that.

## What it is

The site sells itself as an AI writer and copywriting tool, and the headline is volume: over 150 tools, each a single task. A long-form editor handles drafts of 500 words or more from a few variables. The commercial model is unusual in this category, with a free trial and no contract, then a $59 lifetime deal with a 30-day money-back guarantee rather than a monthly subscription.

The site also displays 300+ five-star reviews on AppSumo and says new templates and commands are added weekly. Those are the vendor's own claims, not something independently verified here.

## The template list is the product

Reading the full list is the fastest way to understand what the tool is for, because the specificity is the point. It covers blog production: post titles, outlines, intros, listicle items, listicle-style titles, and bullet points to paragraph. It covers ads and conversion: Facebook and Google ad copy, calls to action. It covers YouTube: keywords to video title, opening lines, random video ideas, video outlines, channel names, descriptions and playlist descriptions. Naming gets business names, band names and book titles. Long-form gets the editor plus book descriptions and author bios.

Then there are the odd but concrete entries, and these say more about the design than the useful ones do: an active-to-passive voice converter, an acronym generator, an analogy built from three words, affirmations, wedding invitation messages, a Wall Street Journal style business article intro, and an AppSumo-style app description. Social gets tweets and threads. Everything else gets an AI image tool, a story generator, an art prompt helper, ask-me-anything, a vision statement and a wildcard.

A general model can do every one of these. The claim being made is not that it does them better, but that you do not have to specify the format each time. That is a real saving if you produce the same formats repeatedly, and a rounding error if you produce each one once.

## Where templates beat a chat box

The argument for this design is consistency. A template fixes the output shape: a blog outline comes back as an outline, an ad request comes back in the platform's format, a YouTube description comes back with the structure YouTube rewards. With a chat box you spend the first two turns explaining what you want and the third correcting the shape.

It also lowers the skill floor. Someone who has never written a listicle post does not need to know what a listicle is to get one. That is the same argument that made [[link:/tools/74|Copy.ai]] and [[link:/tools/22|Writesonic]] popular, and it is a legitimate one.

## Where it costs you

The same design has three predictable costs, and the site does not address any of them.

Output settles into a house style. Templates constrain structure, and constrained structure produces recognisable prose. Anyone who reads a lot of AI-assisted marketing copy can pick out the same rhythms. Budget an editing pass for voice, not just for accuracy.

Template sprawl. More than 150 tools means the average user will use a handful and never open the rest. The list reads impressively and functions as a menu; the practical question is whether the six or seven you need are good, and that depends on the underlying model, which the site does not name.

One price, one bet. No monthly plan is shown on the site, so the lifetime deal is the only route past the trial. That is excellent if you stay, and there is no smaller commitment if you leave.

## The comparison page is dated

The site positions itself against [[link:/tools/18|Jasper]], [[link:/tools/74|Copy.ai]], [[link:/tools/23|Rytr]] and ShortlyAI, and calls itself more affordable with more features. Three of those four are still sold and are reasonable reference points. ShortlyAI is not: Jasper absorbed it years ago and it has not been independently available since. That single line dates the comparison, and it is worth knowing before you treat the page as current market research.

The underlying arithmetic still holds. [[link:/tools/23|Rytr]] and [[link:/tools/74|Copy.ai]] bill monthly, and $59 once against a subscription is the strongest thing this product has.

## Who it fits

It fits a solo operator who produces the same handful of formats on a schedule, whether blog outlines, ad variants or YouTube descriptions, and who would rather pay once than maintain another subscription. It fits people who know what they want and are tired of writing prompts to get it.

It does not fit anyone who needs long-form reasoning, argument, or a voice that sounds like a specific person. Templates produce competent average prose by construction. If the output has to be distinctive, this is the wrong tool, and [[link:/tools/24|QuillBot]] or [[link:/tools/90|Grammarly]] on top of a human draft will serve you better.

## The verdict

Nichesss is not competing on model quality and does not pretend to. It competes on the shape of the work: more than 150 fixed formats, one price, no subscription. If that shape matches how you write, the economics are hard to argue with. If it does not, no number of templates will fix it, and the free trial is the honest way to find out, which is exactly why it exists.
tldr: Nichesss is an AI writer built from more than 150 single-task templates rather than a chat box, plus a long-form editor for 500-word-plus drafts. It sells on price: a free trial, then a $59 lifetime deal with a 30-day refund window, against the monthly subscriptions of Jasper, Copy.ai and Rytr. Templates buy consistency and cost you voice, and its comparison page still lists ShortlyAI, which Jasper absorbed years ago.
